slots.name: Turbopump cycle
slots.role: How the pump that feeds the chamber is driven.

options.name: Gas generator
options.note: A small burner spins the turbine, then its exhaust is dumped overboard. Merlin, Vulcain, F-1.
cons: Throws away 2–3 % of the propellant unburned

options.name: Staged combustion, oxygen-rich
options.note: An oxygen-rich preburner spins the turbine, then all its hot gas burns in the main chamber, so nothing is wasted. Kerosene engines do it this way; hot oxygen eats ordinary metals, so the turbine needs special coatings.
options.restarts: BE-4 relights in flight; RD-180 none

options.name: Expander
options.note: Hydrogen heated in the chamber walls spins the turbine. Gentle and endlessly restartable, but only enough power for a small engine.
cons: Thrust −15 %: the cycle cannot drive a big pump

options.name: Electric pump
options.note: Battery-driven motors spin the pumps. The simplest plumbing there is; the batteries are heavy.

options.name: Pressure-fed (no pump)
options.note: No pump at all: tank pressure pushes propellant into the chamber. Unlimited restarts, but the thick tanks and low pressure cost thrust and Isp.
options.real: AJ10 (Delta II second stage), Apollo SPS

options.name: Full-flow staged combustion
options.note: Two preburners, one fuel-rich and one oxygen-rich, each drive their own pump, and every gram of propellant then burns in the main chamber. The highest pressure and Isp there is, and the hardest engine to build.
pros: Cooler turbines than ordinary staged combustion
options.real: Raptor (SpaceX), the only full-flow engine ever flown

options.name: Combustion tap-off
options.note: A little hot gas is bled from the edge of the main chamber to spin the turbine. No separate gas generator, so fewer parts, but the turbine sees chamber-hot gas.

options.name: Staged combustion, fuel-rich
options.note: A hydrogen-rich preburner spins the turbine (the RS-25 has two, each with its own turbopump), then its warm gas burns in the main chamber. Hydrogen engines do it this way because hot hydrogen is gentle on turbines; with kerosene the fuel-rich gas would clog them with soot.
options.real: RS-25 (Space Shuttle, SLS: 206 bar), RD-0120 (Energia), LE-7A (H-IIA)

options.name: Expander bleed
options.note: As in the expander, hydrogen warmed in the chamber walls spins the turbine, but then it is dumped overboard instead of burned. The turbine can take a bigger pressure drop, so the cycle reaches first-stage thrust, and nothing burns before the chamber, so failures are mild. A hydrogen cycle: the fuel must boil and expand in the walls.
options.real: LE-9 (H3 first stage, 1,471 kN), LE-5B (H-IIA upper stage), BE-3U (New Glenn upper stage)
options.restarts: LE-5B and BE-3U restart in flight

slots.name: Injector
slots.role: The plate that sprays fuel and oxidizer into the chamber.

options.name: Shear coaxial
options.note: Hundreds of elements, each a tube of oxygen inside a ring of fast fuel: the fast fuel shears the oxygen into droplets. Smooth combustion.

options.name: Pintle
options.note: One central element: a pin with a sleeve. Deep throttling, cheap to make, hard to make unstable.

options.name: Impinging jets
options.note: Jets of fuel and oxidizer collide and mix. Simple; prone to rough combustion.

options.name: Swirl coaxial
options.note: Each element spins its propellant into a thin cone round the other, so they mix in a short, steady flame. Staged-combustion engines use it to mix hot gas with liquid.

slots.name: Nozzle extension
slots.role: The lower skirt of the bell and how it is kept from melting.

options.name: Regeneratively cooled
options.note: Fuel runs through channels in the bell wall before it burns, keeping the metal cool and preheating the fuel.
pros: Runs as long as there is fuel

options.name: Radiatively cooled niobium
options.note: A thin skirt of C-103 niobium that simply glows orange and radiates the heat away. Light; only for vacuum.

options.name: Carbon-carbon skirt
options.note: Woven carbon fibre in a carbon matrix: half the mass of metal and happy at 2,000 °C.
pros: +4 s of Isp from a longer bell

options.name: Extendable nozzle
options.note: A second skirt that slides down after staging, so a huge bell fits in a short interstage.
cons: One more mechanism that must work

options.name: Ablative liner
options.note: A nozzle lined with resin and silica that chars and wears away slowly, carrying the heat off with it. No cooling plumbing at all: cheap, heavy, good for one long burn.
cons: Wears away: one long burn only
options.real: RS-68 (Delta IV), LR87 nozzle extension (Titan II)

slots.name: Igniter
slots.role: How the engine is lit, and how many times.

options.name: Spark torch
options.note: A small spark-lit torch in the chamber wall. Restartable as long as there is power.
cons: Needs power and a pilot flow

options.name: Pyrotechnic
options.note: A one-shot cartridge. The simplest igniter; one start only.
cons: A dud cartridge cannot be retried (reliability −0.2 %)

options.name: TEA-TEB slugs
options.note: Chemicals that burst into green flame on contact with oxygen. Reliable relights, limited by how many slugs you carry.

options.name: Pyrophoric start capsule
options.note: A sealed capsule of a fluid that bursts into flame on touching oxygen is pushed into the chamber and the preburner at start. Certain and simple; one capsule per start.
pros: Reliable start, no sparks or wiring (reliability +0.2 %)
cons: +$10k: one sealed capsule and valve per start
options.real: RD-170 (triethylaluminium start capsule), RD-191 (starter fluid that ignites on contact with oxygen)

slots.name: Chamber wall and cooling
slots.role: How the combustion chamber survives gas at more than 3,000 °C.

options.name: Milled cooling channels
options.note: A copper-alloy liner with hundreds of narrow channels cut into it and closed by an outer shell; fuel runs through them before it burns, carrying the heat away.
options.real: RS-25 (NARloy-Z liner, about 390 channels), Raptor, Vulcain

options.name: Brazed tube wall
options.note: The chamber and bell are hundreds of thin tubes brazed side by side; fuel runs down one tube and back up the next. Light and proven, but the brazing is slow hand work and the pressure limit is lower.
options.real: F-1 (178 tubes, Inconel X-750), H-1, J-2, RL10

options.name: Channels plus fuel film
options.note: As well as the channels, a ring of small holes sprays fuel along the inside wall, so a cool layer of vapour hugs the metal. Very safe for the wall, but that fuel burns badly.
options.real: F-1 nozzle extension, cooled by a film of turbine exhaust

options.name: Ablative chamber
options.note: No cooling channels at all: the chamber is lined with resin and silica that chars and wears away, carrying the heat off with it. Cheap and simple, but it erodes, so one long burn is all it gets.

slots.name: Nozzle shape
slots.role: The curve of the nozzle wall that turns hot gas into speed. How wide it opens (the expansion ratio: exit area ÷ throat area) is set by the sea-level or vacuum nozzle.

options.name: Bell
options.note: A curved bell about 80 % as long as a cone of the same opening: the shape almost every engine has used since the 1960s.

options.name: 15° cone
options.note: A straight cone: easy to make, but its exhaust spreads out, so about 1.7 % of the push goes sideways.
options.real: A 15° cone loses (1 − cos 15°) ÷ 2 = 1.7 % of the push sideways (the divergence factor)

options.name: Aerospike
options.note: The gas flows along the outside of a central spike instead of inside a bell, so the outside air shapes the jet and it suits every altitude. Tested many times, never flown to orbit: the spike is heavy and hard to cool.
pros: +6 s of Isp: adapts to altitude
options.real: XRS-2200 linear aerospike for the X-33 (909 kN sea level, Isp 339 / 436.5 s, three built and fired at Stennis, programme ended 2001); a small aerospike rocket flew in 2003 (CSULB); first aerospike lit in flight on a winged craft: POLARIS MIRA-II, 29 October 2024

slots.name: Combustion stability
slots.role: What stops the flame from ringing like a bell and shaking the chamber apart.

options.name: Injector design only
options.note: A well-designed injector keeps the flame steady by itself; most modern engines need nothing more.

options.name: Injector baffles
options.note: Metal walls stand out from the injector face and split the chamber into pockets, so sound waves cannot sweep across it. The F-1 needed them: its early chambers rang at 4,000 cycles a second, and some blew apart.
options.real: F-1 (Project First, early 1960s: baffled injector proven with small bombs set off in the firing chamber)

options.name: Acoustic cavities
options.note: A ring of small tuned pockets round the injector swallows sound at the dangerous pitch, like the silencer of a car exhaust.
options.real: Acoustic absorbers are a standard cure for combustion instability (NASA SP-194, 1972)

slots.name: Propellant grain
slots.role: The shape of the hole cast through the propellant, which sets the thrust curve.

options.name: Star grain
options.note: A star-shaped bore gives steady thrust the whole burn.

options.name: High-thrust grain
options.note: More burning surface: +15 % thrust, a shorter burn, slightly less Isp.

options.name: Long-burn grain
options.note: Less surface, a long gentle burn: −15 % thrust, +3 s Isp.

options.name: Finocyl grain
options.note: A round bore with long fins cut into the aft end: high thrust at liftoff that tapers off through the sound barrier, when the stack is under the most strain.

slots.name: Nozzle
slots.role: Fixed, or swivelling to steer.

options.name: Fixed nozzle
options.note: Bolted straight. The core engine steers.

options.name: Vectoring nozzle
options.note: A flexible seal lets the nozzle swing a few degrees. Needed when the solids give most of the thrust.

options.name: Liquid-injection steering
options.note: A fixed nozzle with a tank of nitrogen tetroxide: squirting it into one side of the exhaust bends the jet. No moving nozzle, but the tank and valves weigh a lot.

slots.name: Shock absorber
slots.role: What soaks up the touchdown.

options.name: Crushable honeycomb
options.note: Aluminium honeycomb that crushes once. Light and certain.

options.name: Hydraulic struts
options.note: Oil and gas struts that reset. Heavier; reusable.

options.name: Telescoping pistons + crush cores
options.note: Each leg is a telescoping piston with a cartridge of aluminium honeycomb inside: the honeycomb takes the hit, and a fresh cartridge resets the leg for the next flight.

slots.name: Foot pads
slots.role: How big the feet are.

options.name: Small pads
options.note: Fine on rock.

options.name: Large pads
options.note: Snowshoes for dust.

options.name: Wide dish feet
options.note: Big shallow dishes with crushable rims: they spread the weight on loose sand and slide instead of digging in on a sideways touchdown.
pros: Lands on soft or sloping ground

slots.name: Touchdown sensors
slots.role: How the ship knows its feet are on the ground, so the engine cuts at the right moment.

options.name: Radar altimeter only
options.note: The computer cuts the engine on the radar height. A gust or a rock can fool it by half a metre.
cons: The engine may cut a little high or a little late

options.name: Contact probes
options.note: Long thin rods hang below the feet. The moment one touches the ground a light comes on and the crew shuts the engine down: "Contact light!"
pros: Engine cuts at the right moment

options.name: Load cells in every leg
options.note: Strain gauges in each leg weigh the ship as it settles. The computer cuts the engine only when all four legs carry weight, so it never shuts down on one foot.

slots.name: Base heat shield
slots.role: What protects the engine bay from the glowing exhaust that swirls back up under the engines.

options.name: Flexible thermal curtains
options.note: Quilted boots of glass and ceramic fabric around the top of each engine let it swivel while closing the gap to the hot outside.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC flexible curtains, Shuttle RS-25 heat-shield blankets

options.name: Rigid base heat shield
options.note: A plate of heat-resistant metal and ceramic across the whole base, with a sealed hole for each engine. Under a cluster the jets heat each other, so this is where it matters most.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC base heat shield, Falcon 9 Block 5 Octaweb heat shield

options.name: No base shield
options.note: Bare beams and plumbing. A single engine in thin air gets away with it; a cluster cooks its own wiring.
options.real: Early sounding rockets; N1's first two launches (1969) ended in fires among the 30 engines of its tail

slots.name: Propellant feed
slots.role: The pipes that bring fuel and oxygen from the tanks to each engine.

options.name: Separate feed lines
options.note: One pipe of each propellant to each engine, opened at ignition and closed at the end.
cons: A leaking engine cannot be cut off from its tank

options.name: Manifold with prevalves
options.note: A ring manifold feeds every engine through its own shut-off valve, so the computer can isolate a failing engine and the rest fly on.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC prevalves, Falcon 9 engine-out shutdowns

slots.name: POGO suppressor
slots.role: Stops the engines and the feed lines from shaking each other like a pogo stick.

options.name: Plain feed lines
options.note: Nothing in the lines. If the thrust shake and the sloshing in the pipes fall in step, the whole stack bounces along its length.

options.name: Gas-filled accumulators
options.note: Small helium-filled chambers on the oxygen lines act as shock absorbers and break the rhythm. Fitted to the Saturn V after Apollo 6 shook at 5 Hz and Apollo 13 nearly tore an engine loose.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC and S-II (after Apollo 6 and 13), Titan II for Gemini

slots.name: Chambers
slots.role: How the booster engine burns its kerosene and oxygen.

options.name: Four chambers, one pump
options.note: Four small chambers fed by one turbopump, plus two swivelling verniers. Korolev chose four small chambers because big ones shook themselves apart.

options.name: One big chamber
options.note: One large chamber and nozzle: lighter and cheaper, but big chambers are prone to combustion instability, which took the F-1 years of tests to cure.

slots.name: Turbine drive
slots.role: What spins the turbopump.

options.name: Hydrogen peroxide steam
options.note: Concentrated hydrogen peroxide flows over a bed of solid catalyst pellets and turns into hot steam that spins the turbine. Separate from the main propellants, so it starts easily.

options.name: Gas generator
options.note: A small burner on the main kerosene and oxygen spins the turbine. No peroxide tank to carry.

slots.name: Hydraulic power
slots.role: Where the oil pressure that pushes the two gimbal rams comes from.

options.name: Hydraulic power unit
options.note: A pump and a gas-charged accumulator keep oil at high pressure for the rams, driven by the engine or by an electric motor.

options.name: Fuel as hydraulic fluid
options.note: High-pressure kerosene from the engine’s own pump drives the rams, then flows back to the pump inlet: no separate oil system. Kerosene engines only, and only while the pump turns.
cons: +$15k: a high-pressure tap and filter on the pump
Kerosene engines only; works only while the engine runs

options.name: Hydrazine power unit
options.note: A small turbine spun by decomposing hydrazine drives the hydraulic pump, independent of the engine, so it can steer a solid booster too.
options.real: Space Shuttle solid boosters (two hydrazine units per booster), Space Shuttle orbiter

slots.name: Field joints
slots.role: How the segments, filled with propellant at the factory, are sealed together at the launch site.

options.name: Redesigned joints, three O-rings
options.note: The joint NASA redesigned after Challenger: a third O-ring, and a tang that hooks into the clevis so the joint stays closed when the motor pressurises.
pros: Seals even on a cold morning
options.real: Shuttle redesigned booster (1988–2011), SLS five-segment booster: three O-rings per field joint

options.name: Original joints, two O-rings
options.note: Pins hold tang and clevis together and two O-rings with putty seal them. Under pressure the joint flexes open a little; on a freezing morning stiff rubber cannot follow it. That is what destroyed Challenger in January 1986.

slots.name: Nozzle and steering
slots.role: How the booster's thrust is pointed.

options.name: Flexible-bearing nozzle
options.note: The nozzle sits on a ring of rubber and steel layers that lets it tilt a few degrees, pushed by two actuators.
options.real: Shuttle and SLS boosters (hydraulic, hydrazine power units), S200 (±8°, electro-hydraulic), P120C (electric)

options.name: Liquid-injection steering
options.note: A fixed nozzle; valves squirt nitrogen tetroxide from a tank on the side into one side of the exhaust and bend the jet.
options.real: Titan III and IV boosters (UA120x, external N₂O₄ nacelle)

options.name: Fixed nozzle
options.note: Bolted straight: the core engine does all the steering.
cons: Reliability −0.3 %: no steering from the booster
options.real: GEM-40 (Delta II; fixed nozzle canted 10°), SRB-3 (H3)

slots.name: Propellant grain
slots.role: The shape of the hole through the propellant, which sets how the thrust changes during the burn.

options.name: Star front, round bore behind
options.note: A many-pointed star in the front segment burns a big surface at liftoff; the round bore of the other segments keeps the thrust even.
options.real: Space Shuttle booster (11-point star in the forward segment)

options.name: Max-Q thrust dip
options.note: The grain is shaped so the thrust drops by about a third around 50 s after liftoff, when the air pushes hardest, then rises again.
options.real: Space Shuttle booster (thrust cut by about a third about 50 s after liftoff)

options.name: Finocyl grain
options.note: A round bore with long fins cut into the aft end: high thrust at liftoff that tapers off through the sound barrier.

slots.role: What protects the engine bay from the glowing exhaust that swirls back up under the engines.

options.note: Quilted boots of glass and ceramic fabric around the top of each engine let it swivel while closing the gap to the hot outside.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC flexible curtains, Shuttle RS-25 heat-shield blankets

options.real: Early sounding rockets; N1's first two launches (1969) ended in fires among the 30 engines of its tail

slots.role: The pipes that bring fuel and oxygen from the tanks to each engine.

options.name: Separate feed lines
options.note: One pipe of each propellant to each engine, opened at ignition and closed at the end.
cons: A leaking engine cannot be cut off from its tank

options.note: A ring manifold feeds every engine through its own shut-off valve, so the computer can isolate a failing engine and the rest fly on.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC prevalves, Falcon 9 engine-out shutdowns

options.name: Plain feed lines

options.name: Gas-filled accumulators
options.note: Small helium-filled chambers on the oxygen lines act as shock absorbers and break the rhythm. Fitted to the Saturn V after Apollo 6 shook at 5 Hz and Apollo 13 nearly tore an engine loose.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC and S-II (after Apollo 6 and 13), Titan II for Gemini

slots.name: Steering the ring
slots.role: How a ring of engines bolted fixed points the rocket.

options.name: Differential throttling
options.note: The flight computer throttles engines on opposite sides of the outer ring up and down to pitch and yaw, and a failed engine is shut down together with the one opposite, so the push stays balanced.
options.real: N1 (1969–72): the outer 24 NK-15s throttled for pitch and yaw; KORD shut engines down in opposite pairs

options.name: Swivelling outer engines
options.note: Actuators swivel the engines of the outer ring, as on the outer engines of the Saturn V first stage. A failed engine no longer takes its opposite partner with it.
pros: A failure costs one engine, not two (reliability +0.4 %)
options.real: Saturn V S-IC and Saturn IB (outer engines gimballed)
